scope: Classical CAN arbitration. Illustrations and Python are deterministic teaching models, not controller simulation.

claims.claim: In CAN arbitration a dominant 0 overrides recessive 1
claims.notes: Transceiver behavior assumed in arbitration mode

claims.claim: Losers transmitting recessive while reading dominant give up sending without destroying winner's frame
claims.notes: Contrasts with arbitrary bit discrepancy outside arbitration

claims.claim: Standard ID 0x100 and 0x200 differ first at the second MSB bit (ID9)
claims.notes: 11-bit standard IDs exactly; SOF not included

claims.claim: For matching 11-bit identifier data frame has RTR dominant 0 and wins against remote RTR recessive 1
claims.notes: Classic CAN only; FD does not permit remote frames

claims.claim: Same first 11 identifier bits: standard remote frame beats extended data frame at IDE after RTR/SRR are both recessive
claims.locator: CAN CC base versus extended frames
claims.notes: Base IDE 0, extended IDE 1; distinction in field grouping explained

claims.claim: Normal arbitration loss is not a bit error and does not by itself increase TEC/REC
claims.locator: CAN Error Handling bit error exception in arbitration
claims.notes: Other faults can still trigger errors

claims.claim: Two simultaneous transmitters with the same arbitration field are not separated by arbitration; differing later data bits may raise bit errors
claims.notes: Actual frames may be identical and indistinguishable at bus level

claims.claim: CAN FD excludes remote frames; CAN XL has a distinct priority identifier/content addressing distinction
claims.locator: CAN CC, CAN FD, CAN XL overview
claims.notes: This chapter's remote-frame examples restricted to classical CAN

claims.claim: Defeated transmitter can re-arbitrate when bus is free; successful delivery is not unconditionally guaranteed
claims.notes: One-shot, queue cancellation, overload and faults are implementation-dependent

claims.claim: Three original drawings show bit dominance, first divergence, and RTR/SRR/IDE precedence
claims.notes: Simplified diagrams; no signal timing or waveform-scale claim
